notes.front: What does the third Kanban practice, improving the workflow, ask of Kanban system members?
notes.back: To keep improving their workflow continuously, for a better balance of effectiveness, efficiency and predictability.
notes.explanation: It starts from an explicit DoW: that is what gets changed, and studying the system shows where to change it.
notes.example: A team sees items wait days for review, changes its review policy, then checks whether flow improved.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: Whose responsibility does the Guide say it is to improve the workflow continuously?
notes.explanation: Given an explicit DoW, the people who deliver value through the system own its improvement.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: Improving the workflow aims at a better balance of effectiveness, efficiency and {{c1::predictability}}.
notes.explanation: These are the same three elements whose balance defines value optimization in “Why Use Kanban”.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: What does the Guide say can guide potential improvements to the DoW?
notes.explanation: Improvements should follow from what the members learn about how work actually flows, for example from their flow data.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: Is reviewing the DoW from time to time a requirement of the Guide?
notes.back: No. The Guide calls it common practice, not a requirement tied to any schedule.
notes.explanation: Teams often review the DoW to discuss and make changes, but the Guide does not mandate when.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: Must changes to the DoW wait for a formal meeting held at a regular cadence?
notes.back: No. Kanban system members can and should make just-in-time changes as the context dictates.
notes.explanation: Waiting for a scheduled meeting would delay improvements the members already know they need.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: Does the Guide require workflow improvements to be small and incremental?
notes.back: No. If the Kanban system members feel a significant change is needed, that is what they should implement.
notes.explanation: The Guide prescribes no size of change; the members judge what their context needs.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: According to the Kanban Pocket Guide, which elements of the DoW are candidates for improvement?
notes.explanation: Work items, states, WIP controls, policies, the SLE and the started and finished points can all be experimented with.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 5 “Options for Improvement”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: If an improvement experiment makes things worse, what does the Pocket Guide advise?
notes.back: Go back to what you were doing before.
notes.explanation: Not every process change will work; the point is to try, keep what helps and undo what doesn't.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 5 “Options for Improvement”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the Pocket Guide, when is changing the SLE probably warranted?
notes.back: Only after some other change to the process, such as a change to one of the DoW elements.
notes.explanation: The SLE describes how the current process performs, so it should move when the process does.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 5 “The Service Level Expectation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After a major process change, roughly how many newly completed items does the Pocket Guide suggest before calculating a new SLE?
notes.back: About 10 items that have completed after the change (a rule of thumb).
notes.explanation: Items finished under the old process no longer describe the new one; not every change needs a new SLE.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 5 “The Service Level Expectation”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Pocket Guide suggest when a team runs out of ideas for improving its process?
notes.back: Expand the Kanban system's boundaries upstream or downstream.
notes.explanation: Moving the started and finished points outward raises new questions about WIP controls, policies and the SLE.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 5 “Started and Finished Points”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After studying its flow data, a team splits one overloaded state into two and adds a policy for handoffs. Which Kanban practice is this?
notes.choices:
A) Defining and visualizing a workflow
B) Actively managing items in a workflow
C) Improving a workflow
notes.choicesExplained: A: the DoW already exists; the team is changing it on the basis of study, which is improvement. B: nothing here acts on a particular item in progress.
notes.explanation: Continual study of the system guiding changes to the DoW is exactly what the third practice describes.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: An external auditor offers to decide each quarter which workflow changes a Kanban team should make. What does the Guide say about who improves the workflow?
notes.back: It is the Kanban system members' responsibility to continuously improve their workflow.
notes.choices:
A) The auditor, since outside views are more objective
B) The Kanban system members
C) Whoever owns the Kanban board tool
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide places responsibility with the members; outside input may help, but the responsibility stays theirs. C: the Guide assigns nothing to tool owners.
notes.explanation: Members may seek advice, but continual improvement is theirs, and a quarterly schedule is not required either.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: A team compares how long its last 30 items took and finds most delay sits in one handoff. What does the Guide say this kind of study can guide?
notes.explanation: The Guide says continual study of the system can guide improvements, such as changing the policy for that handoff.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: Mid-month, a team sees its test queue growing fast. The coach says: note it and wait for the quarterly process review. What does the Guide say?
notes.back: Don't wait: members can and should make just-in-time changes to the DoW as the context dictates.
notes.choices:
A) Wait: DoW changes belong in the scheduled review
B) Change the DoW now if the context calls for it
C) Only the SLE may change between reviews
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says there is no requirement to wait for a formal meeting at a regular cadence. C: the Guide puts no such limit on what can change.
notes.explanation: Reviewing the DoW from time to time is common practice, but it is not a gate for changes.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: A team concludes its whole workflow needs redesigning, but a manager insists on one small tweak at a time. Does the Guide back the manager?
notes.back: No. The Guide does not prescribe small, incremental changes; a significant change is right if the members feel it is needed.
notes.explanation: Nothing in the Guide limits the size of an improvement.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7

notes.front: What is the difference between reviewing the active items and reviewing the DoW?
notes.back: Reviewing active items is active management of work in progress; reviewing the DoW is about improving the workflow itself.
notes.explanation: Neither review is tied to a required meeting or cadence in the Guide.
notes.contrast: Look at the work now versus change the rules the work follows.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Improving the Workflow”, p. 7
